content.text: Why does a bicycle tyre feel harder on a hot day? Why does a balloon shrink in a cold room? The behaviour of gases can be explained using the kinetic particle model. Understanding how pressure, volume, and temperature are related is essential for explaining many everyday phenomena.

Gas pressure is caused by gas particles colliding with the walls of their container. The pressure depends on how often particles hit the walls (frequency of collisions) and how hard they hit (force of each collision).
Gas pressure is caused by gas particles colliding with the walls of their container.
Particles move randomly at high speeds
Each collision exerts a tiny force
Billions of collisions per second create measurable pressure
Collisions are harder (more force per collision)
Same number of particles in smaller space
If you decrease the volume, pressure increases (and vice versa).

attrs.alt: Boyle's law graphs showing pressure vs volume (hyperbola) and pressure vs 1/volume (straight line)

content.text: If you increase the temperature, volume increases (gas expands).
If you increase the temperature, pressure increases.

When using gas law equations, temperature must always be in kelvin, not Celsius. Using Celsius temperatures in gas law calculations will give incorrect answers. Always convert first: T(K) = T(degrees C) + 273.

Boyle's law (pV = constant at constant T) and the pressure law (p/T = constant at constant V) can be combined: p1V1/T1 = p2V2/T2. This combined gas law covers all situations where two of the three variables change.
A gas has volume 2 m³ at pressure 100 kPa. If the volume is reduced to 0.5 m³ at constant temperature, what is the new pressure?
A balloon has volume 500 cm³ at 20°C. What is its volume at 60°C if pressure is constant?
A fixed volume of gas has pressure 200 kPa at 27°C. What is the pressure at 127°C?
A gas at 100 kPa and 300 K occupies 2 m³. Find its volume at 150 kPa and 400 K.
Why does a balloon expand when heated?
Particles collide with walls more frequently and harder
Higher inside pressure pushes walls outward
Balloon expands until inside pressure equals outside pressure
Why does a car tyre feel harder on a hot day?
When temperature increases, particles move faster
More frequent and harder collisions with tyre walls
Higher pressure makes the tyre feel harder
Why does a deodorant can warn against heating?
If heated, pressure inside increases rapidly (P ∝ T)
Can may not withstand the increased pressure
(0 K = -273°C) is the theoretical temperature at which:
Pressure of an ideal gas would be zero
If we plot pressure vs temperature and extend the line, it crosses zero pressure at -273°C.

content.text: Higher pressure raises boiling point of water
Food cooks faster at higher temperature
When valve opens, high-pressure gas escapes
Divers must account for pressure changes
Surfacing too fast is dangerous (decompression sickness)
— Pressure acts in all directions equally.
— You must use kelvin! Doubling °C doesn't double K.
"Gases can be cooled to absolute zero"
— Absolute zero can never actually be reached, only approached.
"Compressing a gas heats it because you're adding energy"
— You're doing work on the gas, which increases its internal energy.
"At constant temperature, gas particles don't move faster when compressed"
— Correct! They just collide with walls more often (same speed, smaller space).
Calculate the pressure of a gas when its volume is increased from 3 m³ to 6 m³ at constant temperature. The initial pressure is 80 kPa.
Calculate the temperature (in °C) at which a balloon's volume reaches 1.5 litres, given that it has a volume of 1 litre at 20°C and constant pressure.
Calculate the pressure of a gas at 75°C in a fixed volume, given that its pressure is 100 kPa at 25°C.
Explain, using the kinetic particle model, why pressure increases when a gas is compressed at constant temperature.
Calculate the new pressure when a syringe containing 20 cm³ of gas at 100 kPa is compressed to a volume of 5 cm³.
Explain why aerosol cans should never be thrown into a fire.
Calculate the new pressure in a car tyre after a long drive, given that it was inflated to 200 kPa at 17°C and the temperature has risen to 47°C. Assume the volume does not change significantly.
Gas pressure is caused by particle collisions with container walls
Pressure increases with: higher temperature, smaller volume, more gas
Always use kelvin for temperature in gas law calculations
Absolute zero (0 K = -273°C) is the lowest possible temperature
Applications: pressure cookers, aerosols, diving, weather
— Using Boyle's Law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. 80 × 3 = P₂ × 6. P₂ = 240/6 = 40 kPa (calculation)
— Convert to kelvin: T₁ = 20 + 273 = 293 K. Using Charles's Law: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. 1/293 = 1.5/T₂. T₂ = 1.5 × 293 = 439.5 K. In °C: 439.5 − 273 = 166.5°C ≈ 167°C (calculation)
— Convert to kelvin: T₁ = 25 + 273 = 298 K, T₂ = 75 + 273 = 348 K. Using P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂: 100/298 = P₂/348. P₂ = (100 × 348)/298 = 116.8 kPa ≈ 117 kPa (calculation)
When a gas is compressed at constant temperature, the same number of particles occupy a smaller volume.

The particles travel shorter distances between collisions with the walls, so they hit the walls more frequently. Since the temperature is constant, each collision has the same average force. More frequent collisions on the same area of wall means greater pressure. (explanation with physics reasoning)
— Using Boyle's Law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. 100 × 20 = P₂ × 5. P₂ = 2000/5 = 400 kPa (calculation)
An aerosol can contains gas under pressure in a fixed volume.

In a fire, the temperature increases dramatically. Since P is proportional to T (at constant volume), the pressure inside the can rises rapidly. The can is not designed to withstand very high pressures, so it may rupture or explode violently, which is extremely dangerous. (explanation with physics reasoning)
— Convert to kelvin: T₁ = 17 + 273 = 290 K, T₂ = 47 + 273 = 320 K. Using P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂: 200/290 = P₂/320. P₂ = (200 × 320)/290 = 220.7 kPa ≈ 221 kPa (calculation)
